---
title: "Everyday life"
subtitle: "Church on Sunday, seniors midweek, and a long ride to work"
---

Everyday life in Adamsville runs on a few strong anchors (churches, the recreation centers, the skating rink) and on a shared norm of privacy. That norm protects quiet but also limits collective action.

## The rhythm of the week and year

| When | What happens | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Sunday | Church services; the elders are "a lot" at church. Food center open 9 a.m.–1 p.m. | Resident B; ACFB |
| Weekdays | Average commute of 34 minutes; about 1 in 6 workers rides transit. Pool open 8 a.m.–7 p.m. at C. T. Martin | ACS 2020–2024; City of Atlanta DPR |
| Wednesday–Friday | Seniors gather at the old Adamsville Recreation Center | Resident A; NPU-H Master Plan |
| Monday–Thursday | Food center open by appointment, client choice | Atlanta Community Food Bank |
| Weekends | Events at Wilson Mill Park and churches; skating at Cascade | Residents A and B |
| Monthly | NPU-H meeting at C. T. Martin Recreation Center | City of Atlanta |
| Each year | National Night Out; Mays High homecoming; church back-to-school giveaways | Residents A and B |

## Anchors

**Churches.** Resident A counted four churches near her block. Resident B said the elders "are involved in church a lot on Sundays. That's where they're going." Churches also run back-to-school drives and giveaways that, as Resident A noted, mostly serve people who are not members. The civic role of churches has deep roots here: in 1955 the Civic Club proposed that ministers lead a citizens' committee to help neighbors in need.

**Recreation.** The C. T. Martin Natatorium and Recreation Center at 3201 MLK Jr. Drive has a 50-meter pool and a warm-water therapy pool (City of Atlanta Department of Parks and Recreation, n.d.). It was built after council member C. T. Martin pushed to demolish a troubled apartment complex, and was renamed for him in 2017 (The Atlanta Voice, 2021). The older Adamsville Recreation Center serves seniors and works as a warming center (City of Atlanta & TSW, 2020, p. 18). Cascade Family Skating, featured in the 2006 film *ATL*, draws young people from across the region. Community events happen mostly at Wilson Mill Park and churches.

**Gardens and food.** Young Generation Movement, a youth nonprofit named in the master plan alongside Gratitude Botanical Farm (City of Atlanta & TSW, 2020, p. 42), runs a community garden and marketplace. Resident A said the garden gives young people "a productive and safe place to go."

## Norms

::: {.voice .b}
"Nobody bothered anybody, which is actually what I like about it… That also is like the reason why some people don't cut their grass."
<span class="who">Resident B, interview, October 19, 2026</span>
:::

Asked about unwritten rules, Resident B described one: leave people alone. Privacy is valued, especially by older homeowners who remember a rural past, and it makes Adamsville feel calm. It also has costs. Neighbors do not organize around overgrown lots, and many residents, as Resident A said, "just go home, wake up, go to work," missing news about meetings or events. Both residents suggested old-fashioned fixes: flyers, a magnet in every mailbox, door knocking, a newsletter.

Care between neighbors happens one to one rather than through organizations: gifts dropped off, packages picked up, a cat rehomed next door. Adamsville has strong personal ties and weak organizational ones. That explains both why residents feel at home and why turnout at public meetings is low.

## Two residents, one conversation

Placed side by side, the interviews read like a conversation about the same streets.

::: {.dialogue}
<div class="bubble a">"I will say Adamsville is a bit of a food desert, honestly… You would have to go a couple exits up."<small>Resident A</small></div>
<div class="bubble b">"If I had to walk, I would not be able to get to those places. What I can walk to is a KFC and a Taco Bell and a Checkers."<small>Resident B</small></div>
<div class="bubble a">"Oh, I didn't know we had an NPU-H… So it's like a lot of people just aren't in the know."<small>Resident A</small></div>
<div class="bubble b">"It's kind of like pulling teeth to get people to go or to participate."<small>Resident B</small></div>
<div class="bubble a">"They're just redoing the homes and putting them up for rent, like Airbnb."<small>Resident A</small></div>
<div class="bubble b">"I want it to look more contemporary, like some newer renovations on the houses."<small>Resident B</small></div>
:::

The last exchange shows a real disagreement. One resident sees renovation as investors extracting value; the other sees it as long-awaited improvement.

## Getting around

About one in four NPU-H households has no car, and 16 percent of workers commute by transit, nearly three times the city rate. Resident B, who drives, can walk only to fast food. The Civic Club's 1955 hope for "natural walkways" linking homes to schools and stores was never built, and in 2026 many streets still lack sidewalks. Resident B recalled being told that her subdivision was built without sidewalks on purpose. People walk in the street or not at all.
